# SK1090 — Use a computed property instead of an auto-property holding a constant

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A get-only auto-property is initialized to a compile-time constant and assigned nowhere else, so it is that constant.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | hint |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | 6.0 |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

An auto-property that can only ever hold one compile-time constant is a constant with storage bolted to it: the type carries a field for it, every instance pays for the field, and every constructor writes the same value into every one of them. `=> expr` says the same thing with no field and no write, and the compiler folds the constant at each read. The `SK1xxx` premise applies directly — the auto-property-with-initializer shape is what most of the training data contains, because it is the shape that has been idiomatic longest.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
sealed class Endpoint {
    public string Scheme { get; } = "https";
}
```

Write:

```csharp
sealed class Endpoint {
    public string Scheme => "https";
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Only a get-only auto-property (`{ get; }`), and that restriction is the whole reason this rule can exist at all.** An auto-property is part of the type's layout and a serializer or a source generator writes it by reflection with no attribute to announce that it is doing so — Newtonsoft.Json writes a private setter by default — so converting a *settable* auto-property to a computed one silently changes what deserialization produces, and that is the wall this concept has hit before. A get-only auto-property is different in kind rather than in degree: its backing field is emitted `initonly`, .NET Core's `FieldInfo.SetValue` refuses an init-only field, and there is therefore no reflection path that writes it. ⚠ **The initializer must be a compile-time constant**, decided by Roslyn's own constant folding rather than by a shape list. That is what makes re-evaluating it on every read the same program: a constant read twice is the same value and costs nothing, whereas `public List<int> Items { get; } = new();` turned into `=> new()` would hand every caller a different list. A `typeof`, a `static readonly` reference and a call are all declined for the same reason — none of them is a constant. ⚠ **Nothing may assign the property.** A get-only auto-property is assignable from the declaring type's constructors, and the fix would turn that into CS0200, so every assignment in the type is looked for and any one of them withdraws the finding. The containing type must therefore be declared in exactly one file: a `partial` type split across files has assignments this analysis cannot see. ⚠ **Classes only.** In a struct the backing field is the struct's size, and removing it changes `sizeof`, interop marshalling and every blittable assumption made about the layout. Records are excluded on the same principle — the synthesized members are written against the fields. ⚠ A property carrying an attribute, or living in a type carrying `[Serializable]` or `[StructLayout]`, is declined: those are the declarations most likely to be read reflectively. `abstract`, `extern`, `partial` and `required` properties are excluded, as is any span holding a comment or a preprocessor directive.
